questions_and_answers.question: In German, when the infinitive form of a verb is used as a noun, what gender does it have?

answers.answer: It is always a plural noun

questions_and_answers.question: Which of the following English gerund nouns best illustrates the German use of infinitives as nouns?
Why must regular adjective endings be added to the stem ander- in German?

answers.answer: Because there is no endingless citation form for this adjective
Because adjectives always end in -en regardless of context
Because the specifier is always plural
Because it copies the English adjective ending

questions_and_answers.question: What must accompany the verb 'stellen' ('to put') in German?

answers.answer: A prepositional phrase or the word 'hin'

questions_and_answers.question: Can the verb 'stellen' occur without a complement?
What does the verb 'passen' mean when used with the preposition 'zu' (as in Unit 7)?
In the notes, why is 'passen' considered equivalent to 'stellen' in its influence on grammar?

answers.answer: Because both verbs determine the accusative case for the noun phrase following a two-way preposition
Because they both mean to eat
Because they only use the dative case

questions_and_answers.question: Which verb is reflexive and typically needs a prepositional phrase like 'an den Tisch'?
In the reflexive verb 'sich setzen', what does the reflexive pronoun refer to?
Why are the verbs 'passen' and 'stellen' listed separately in the notes?

answers.answer: Because they have different English equivalents depending on context
Because one is reflexive and the other is not
Because they always use dative case

articles.text:
The infinitive form of many verbs can be used as a noun in German. It is always a das-noun. English has similar nouns, like playing, working, speaking, etc., but often uses the infinitive in equivalent sentences.

This adjective always has an ending of some kind, in this case the ending that the specifier-adjective-noun sequence den anderen Zimmern requires. There is no endingless citation form, but regular adjective endings are added to the stem ander-.

The verb stellen "to put" is complemented either by a prepositional phrase such as an die Wand or by the word hin. It does not occur without a complement, however.

This is actually the same verb as was encountered in Unit 4 in the form es passt mir "it suits me, it's convenient for me" and as occurs later on in this unit with the preposition zu, meaning "to match, to go (with)". Because of the divergent English equivalents in different situations the verb is listed separately each time. In this sentence the implication is that the table will end up in front of the two chairs when it has been put there; in its grammatical influence on the syntactic environment (vor die beiden Sessel, accusative) it is equivalent to the verb stellen "to put".

The verb sich setzen "to sit down" is usually complemented by a prepositional phrase such as an den Tisch or by the word hin.
